tagline: A campaign for bicycle shoulders became a lake-country drive with Bunyan lore.
intro: The Paul Bunyan Scenic Byway follows 54 miles of county roads in a double loop through Minnesota lake country. Broad paved shoulders accompany the drive through lakes and forests. The Federal Highway Administration lists 1.5 hours to drive it, or four to six hours to explore. The byway association says its successful 2005 national designation application emphasized family resorts and the nationally known Paul Bunyan tall tales. Twelve interpretive panel kiosks are spread through the byway, and the association’s Crosslake exhibit collects Bunyan souvenirs and historic advertising.

A bicycle-safety campaign set the byway project in motion. In 1995, Ideal Township residents held a raffle to help pay for paved shoulders on County State Aid Highway 16. A state tourism representative suggested scenic designation could move the work up the county’s priority list. Residents prepared the application, won state designation in June 1998 and saw the shoulder paving finished in August 2002.

For the Crosslake-to-Pequot Lakes portion, Crosslake introduces the logging past: the Pine River Dam was built in 1885, and the growing logging industry drew early residents. Continue through Breezy Point, the resort community on Pelican Lake, to Pequot Lakes, where Bean Hole Days brings the town’s July gathering.

moments.title: Crosslake
moments.text: A nearly thirteen-foot Paul Bunyan rag doll has his own wooden chair in Crosslake’s byway exhibit. The byway association identifies him as a former Guinness record holder for the world’s largest rag doll. The association tells the story of collector Wayne Chamberlain spotting the doll on eBay and contacting its owner; Paul and his chair became a donation. The exhibit is in the Corps of Engineers office at Cross Lake Recreation Area, south of Crosslake on County Road 66. Other pieces include postcards, advertising items and Bunyan piggybanks. He is jointed, like a Cabbage Patch doll.

moments.title: Breezy Point
moments.text: Breezy Point’s resort beginnings remain legible in the Wilford H. Fawcett House, a historic residence built from peeled Norway pine logs. Fawcett, creator of Captain Billy’s Whiz Bang, hired Minneapolis architects Magney and Tusler to design his private house in the Swiss Chateau style. The house has a Y-shaped plan, with a circular staircase leading to a reading balcony in the central hall. The resort’s large log lodge burned, but the house survives. The growing resort community incorporated as Pelican Lakes in 1939 and took the name Breezy Point in 1969.

moments.title: Pequot Lakes
moments.text: In Pequot Lakes, the bean pots have names: Ole and Sven are among the Scandinavian names given to vessels used for Bean Hole Days. The July festival began in 1938, when town shopkeepers hosted a bean feed for local farmers. Beans cook in pots set in pits, a practice that remains the center of the annual gathering. Over the years, the event has added a Bean Hole Days king and queen. The named pots and royal titles grew out of that original shared meal offered by the town’s store owners.
